title: Measure a sprout every morning for a week
description: A sprout on a windowsill grows whether you watch or not — but measure it every morning and the week turns into a chart, a race and a small lesson in how living things actually grow: in spurts.

body.heading: Set up the race
paragraphs: Plant fast seeds — beans or cress — in a clear cup against damp paper or soil, so roots show as well as shoots. Mark day one with a ruler photograph: seed, date, and the height of anything green, even if the honest answer is zero.

Measure at the same time each morning, from the soil line to the tip of the tallest leaf, and write the number in a table before you water. Same time, same method — that is what makes it science rather than impressions.

body.heading: Read the week's story
paragraphs: Most sprouts do nothing, then leap. Growth comes in spurts tied to water, warmth and light, and your chart will show flat days and sudden jumps rather than a smooth staircase.
At week's end, graph the numbers: days across, height up. You have grown two things — a plant, and a record no memory could have kept as honestly.

takeaway: Measure one sprout at the same time every morning for a week and graph it: growth arrives in spurts, and the chart proves what memory would smooth away.
materials: A clear cup, soil or damp paper
A notebook for the daily table
supervision: An adult should supervise planting and watering near windowsills and keep seeds away from very young children who might eat them.
safetyNotes: Use untreated seeds sold for sprouting or planting.
Keep the cup where it cannot be knocked into food areas.
